shorts.title: Ravne league final
shorts.detail: A stretch of the 2015 Slovenian women's national league final.

editorialComments.body: Watch the purple-shirted player's first recovery step here. The feet are visible from the side.
The late scoreboard cut shows 10–8. The excerpt gives the score at that moment and then goes back to play.
The receiving player in pink stays visibly low while waiting. Try comparing her head height before and during the point.
The coaching cutaway is brief, but it shows another part of the match that highlight reels often leave out.
The near player's feet are the clearest thing in this shot. Follow those if the ball is hard to pick out.
The last angle is almost level with the table. Compare it with the opening view for a sense of net height.
The opening angle puts the end line right in view. Watch how much room each player leaves behind it.
The pink-shirted player has a staggered stance in the opening exchange. It's worth watching the feet here.
Watch the recovery after the first swing. The paddle comes back in front before the players reset.
At the end of the point, both players drift back toward the table rather than waiting from where they finished.
The tight scoreboard shot gives you a quick breather after watching from courtside.
I like that they kept the manual scoreboard in the edit. It's part of the atmosphere of a league match.
Use the cutaway to look for the boundaries of the playing area. The blue barriers sit fairly close behind the table.
The break between exchanges makes the next serve setup easier to spot.
When they cut back to the table, watch the player in purple settle before the point starts.
Look at the gap between the players and the end lines. The side angle makes it easier to judge than a head-on shot.
Watch the return to ready position here, not just the contact. That's the part I'd take into practice.
The crowd is right behind the barrier. This angle gives a good sense of the room without losing the table.
The framing changes here. Pick out the table corners first so the next exchange is easier to follow.
Notice how the blue surrounds make the white edge lines easy to see when the shot changes.
The near player is already down in a wide base as the opponent bends over the table.
This angle is useful for comparing how much each player leans forward before contact.
A good spot to watch the free arm. It's easy to miss what it does when you're following the ball.
The two players' distances from the table change during the point. The wide shot lets you see both adjustments.
I'd replay this exchange once watching only the pink-shirted player, then again watching only her opponent.
The wide shot shows where the players and officials are positioned around the table.

shorts.title: Netherlands vs China
shorts.detail: A 1977 international match in Heerjansdam, preserved in Dutch newsreel footage.

editorialComments.body: The near player takes a notably wide step across the floor. The full-body framing makes it easy to catch.
Several spectators are clapping in the close-up. The clip gives them a moment before returning to the table.
The player at the far end is visibly low and ready. The white shoes make the stance easy to spot.
The edit shifts from play to a close-up of people at courtside. It feels more like a newsreel than a match broadcast.
The near-side player moves toward the left edge of the shot. Notice how that changes the angle back to the table.
Both players and most of the floor are in frame. It's a good starting point if you want to study recovery steps.
The opening shot keeps the audience just beyond the net. The hall feels smaller than a modern arena.
The ball can be hard to separate from the table in the first shot. Watching the paddles is easier.
The dark floor and bright court lines make this a useful clip for watching foot placement.
The camera is almost level with the table here. Look at the player beyond the net rather than the foreground.
Watch the space between the far player's elbow and body. The closer framing makes the preparation easier to see.
The perspective changes to show both ends. This is where it gets easier to compare the two players' spacing.
Those lines belong to the hall floor. They're a useful reference for how far each player travels off center.
The near-side player's shoes stay easy to see even when the ball blends into the background.
Try watching just the first step after contact. The camera holds the shot long enough to do that.
The wide view makes it clear how much of the court a player can cover without leaving the frame.
The hall seating is close enough that you can see heads turn as the point moves from side to side.
The return to the middle is worth a second look. It sets up the next stroke before the ball gets there.
There's no need to guess spin from this footage. The feet and body positions are much easier to read.
Compare where the far player stands between points with where he ends up during an exchange.
The near player is back by the end line here. Use the floor markings to judge the difference from the previous rally.
This is a good stretch to watch the far-side player's readiness while the other player moves.
I like the steady camera here. You can follow the pace without a cut at every stroke.
Look at the table and floor together. From this angle you get a better idea of how far out the players move.
The cut to the crowd is worth leaving in. It gives the match a sense of place.
Coming back from the crowd shot, pick up the far player first to get your bearings.
The wide view returns in time to show the far player close to the end of the table.
Watch the near player's shoulders in the next exchange. They stand out more clearly than the ball.
Both ends stay visible as the player in the foreground comes forward again.
The final audience shots are as much a part of this excerpt as the rallies. They show how the event was filmed.

shorts.title: A game between brothers
shorts.detail: A courtside view of a real game recorded in a covered courtyard.

editorialComments.body: The tiled floor gives this clip a built-in footwork grid. It helps make small adjustments visible.
The camera tilts as the near player steps across it. The tabletop is partly hidden for a moment.
The far-side player is framed by the open side of the courtyard. The daylight makes that end easier to see.
Pause here and look at the gap between the table leg and the near player's feet. There isn't much room behind him.
The last clear view of the far side shows the other player still by the table as the phone settles.
Watch the white-shirted player's stance rather than trying to track the ball through the whole clip.
The phone is just behind the near player. You get a good look at how much room there is to move.
The table is close to the camera. The net and side line are useful reference points when the phone tilts.
The near player's shoes come into view. The tiles make it easy to judge the width of his steps.
The two ends are lit differently. The far side stays brighter, which makes the position of the other player clearer.
The far player is back in view as the near player shifts to the edge of the frame.
It feels like standing just off the court. The phone moves when the near player gets close.
The table stays in much the same place in the shot. Use its corner to see how much the player has moved.
The far end is easy to spot when the near player moves aside. That's a better moment to watch the other side.
When the camera dips, the net is still in view. It's a good landmark to follow if you lose the players for a moment.
Watch the space to either side of the near player. His movement is easier to see than the ball in this framing.
The bright area behind the far player and the shade over the near end give the two sides a very different look.
This is a useful example of how a close camera can make a small movement look much bigger.
I had to watch this section twice. The near player's legs are much easier to follow than the paddle.
As the table comes back into view, look for the far player's ready position.
The table edge cuts diagonally across the frame. It makes the small space around the table feel even tighter.
A good clip for watching how people reset in a small space. The camera is too close to judge every stroke.

shorts.title: Table tennis outdoors
shorts.detail: Players trade shots on an improvised outdoor table.

editorialComments.body: The light-colored paddle on the right is easier to pick out than the ball.
The glance toward the camera makes this feel like a real gathering around a game.
The near end briefly clears, giving a better view of how the wooden base is put together.
The player in blue shorts is back at the right end. His paddle is easy to see against the background.
Both ends of the table are visible again. Compare how close the two players keep their feet to it.
The camera keeps the spectators in frame. You can see how the court doubles as a place to hang out.
The wooden table is the first thing I noticed. There's very little extra room at either end.
The camera stands at a corner, so you can see the table and the people gathered around it in the same shot.
Look at the space between the left side of the table and the people watching. It stays pretty narrow.
The player on the right opens his stance as he faces the table. His legs are easy to see from this angle.
The table edge makes a good reference for how close the players stand to it.
As people move around the corner, the camera stays pointed at the same part of the table.
The plaid-shirted spectator moves into the foreground. For a second you can see what watching from that corner is like.
The group in the background stays close while the people near the table trade places.
The camera follows the movement at the near edge without losing sight of the tabletop.
At this angle it's easier to see where the players stand than to tell exactly where each ball lands.
There's a clear look at the table and the space around it when the foreground opens up.
The player at the far side is partly framed by the shaded area. Follow the pale table edge to keep your bearings.
The camera goes back to the table quickly. You can follow the scene without needing to know the score.
The darker shirt on the left stands out against the light ground. That helps when you're watching the first step.
Watch the near corner of the table as the people to the left shift position.
The table looks different from the one in the league clip, but the small reset before an exchange is familiar.
The final wide view shows how closely everyone fits around the table and still leaves room for play.
This angle is a reminder that you can learn from spacing and positioning even when a clip isn't sharp enough to read spin.

courses.title: Find your ready position
courses.detail: Reset between shots and find a stance you can move from.
steps: Stand a short step behind the end line. Hold the paddle in front and bend your knees until a small side step feels easy.
Have a partner hold up a hand to signal left or right. Move a half step in that direction and return to the middle. Switch roles after ten signals.
Ask for ten gentle feeds. After each stroke, check that the paddle returns in front of your body before the next ball arrives.

courses.title: Build a repeatable forehand
courses.detail: Work on contact timing and recovery before adding pace.
steps: Start with ten drop feeds to your forehand. Use a compact swing and contact the ball in front of your body near the top of its bounce.
Ask a partner to block your cross-court drive. Pick a broad target and play two rounds of ten at a speed you can repeat.
Play another ten feeds. Pause if you miss twice in a row and check whether your feet or your swing started late.
Increase pace for three balls only after landing seven out of ten. Return to the original rhythm if the ball starts flying long.

courses.title: Keep the backhand push low
courses.detail: Develop a reliable return against a short backspin feed.
steps: Have a partner feed slow backspin to your backhand. Step toward the ball with the paddle in front of you.
Angle the face open and brush underneath the ball with a compact motion. Start cross-court, where the target is wider.
Alternate a shorter touch and a deeper push in pairs. Ask your partner to call out whether the second bounce would land on the table.
Repeat ten feeds and count only returns that cross low and land in your chosen zone.

courses.title: Move and recover
courses.detail: Keep your balance while moving between two forehand positions.
steps: Mark two comfortable forehand positions a short step apart. Shadow a compact swing in each spot for 30 seconds.
Ask for alternating feeds to the two spots. Keep your weight balanced and arrive before you begin each stroke.
Have your partner feed twice to one spot before switching. Recover after every ball so the change does not catch you leaning.
Do three rounds of 40 seconds with a rest between rounds. Record the longest streak in which you stayed balanced.

courses.title: Place the short serve
courses.detail: Control the length of a backspin serve and plan your next shot.
steps: Practice a legal toss from an open palm. Keep the ball visible to the receiver throughout the motion.
Brush beneath the ball and watch where the first bounce lands on your side. Vary only that placement over two sets of five.
Leave the return alone and count how many serves would bounce twice on the far side. Choose a target where you can repeat the result.
Ask a partner to return five serves. Reset your feet immediately after each serve and prepare for a short return.

courses.title: Read length before spin
courses.detail: Choose a balanced first response before the rally accelerates.
steps: Ask a partner to alternate an obvious short serve and a deep serve. Call the length as soon as you can judge the bounce.
Add a gentle push for short backspin and a compact drive for a long topspin feed. Aim for a broad target to establish control.
Let your partner choose the order. Track which serves you read correctly before scoring the quality of the return.
Play six practice points. After each point, name the cue that led to your choice and change only one thing for the next return.
